newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Breakthrough seen in Colombian truckers' strike.
newsitem.headline: Breakthrough seen in Colombian truckers' strike.

text.p: Colombian truck drivers said talks with the government were going well and that there could be an agreement by late Thursday to end their 11-day strike which has paralyzed key sectors of the economy.

"Our negotiations are on the right path and we're hopeful there may be a breakthrough by the end of today," said Jorge Cuellar, an executive director of the independent Colombian Truck Drivers' Association.

Heads of the association were huddled in negotiations with Transport Minister Carlos Hernan Lopez and Interior Minister Horacio Serpa since the morning and Cuellar said the session could last until 2200 local time/0300 GMT.

One of the truckers' central demands is a 30 percent raise in cargo rates and an end to a ban imposed by some transport companies on the use of vehicles more than 11 years old. The government has so far offered a 15 percent hike in freight rates.

Association members, who work in the private sector and have no contractual obligations directly to the government, defied a government order Friday to return to work after it declared their strike illegal.

Serpa followed this Wednesday by unveiling a package of tough measures designed to break the truckers' strike, including a call to police and the military to immediately clear any road blocks set up by strikers. He also ordered provincial governors and mayors to take all steps deemed necessary to reestablish transport services.

There were no reports of major incidents between truckers and the security forces Thursday, although local TV news reported the arrest of at least one driver who defied police orders to move his vehicle on the highway from Bogota to the eastern plains.
Television reports also showed 40 trucks partially blocking the highway to Colombia's main Pacific coast port of Buenaventura.

Colombia's influential National Coffee Growers' Federation said earlier this week that more than 250,000 60-kg sacks of coffee, quarter of the total promised for October delivery, had been delayed by the strike.
Other key export products such as bananas and coal have also been paralyzed, together with the supply of basic foodstuffs to some major cities.
